claims.text: The target alloy is initially a homogeneous, single-phase, compositionally complex high-entropy alloy, exemplified by a CrCoNi-type system.
Combined high temperature, high strain rate, and prolonged dwell induce nanoscale grain-boundary chemical fluctuations in the target alloy.
The induced grain-boundary chemical fluctuations consist of trace-element segregation or nanoclustering without overt intermetallic precipitation.
Nanoscale grain-boundary segregation locally reduces grain-boundary cohesive strength.
Segregated grain boundaries provide preferred sites for crack initiation.
The resulting brittle failure mechanism is distinct from conventional-alloy embrittlement by gross segregation or brittle grain-boundary precipitation.
High temperature and high strain rate enhance atomic mobility in the high-entropy alloy.
High-entropy-alloy chemistry suppresses gross brittle intermetallic precipitation during the proposed transition.
Grain-boundary nanosegregation appears before and accompanies the transition to brittle behavior.
The transition produces intergranular cracking and a lower strain to failure than the initial baseline.
Under milder temperature and strain-rate conditions, the high-entropy alloy deforms uniformly and ductilely without significant grain-boundary segregation.
Conventional alloys become brittle only after well-developed segregation and precipitate formation.
At low temperatures or very slow loading rates, the target alloy retains both ductility and a homogeneous microstructure.
The proposed nanosegregation-mediated embrittlement is confined to high-temperature, high-strain-rate service regimes.
Grain-boundary impurity segregation and grain-boundary second-phase precipitation are established causes of cohesion loss or crack initiation in conventional metals and alloys.
